claim: The final leg of the Jackson Park elevated branch to Jackson Park was built directly over 63rd Street rather than in alleys.
evidence: Sibling graded VERIFIED; unusual engineering choice making the street itself a transit corridor.
notes: Precondition claim for the transit-spine function.

claim: 63rd & Halsted was 'the second busiest shopping district/commercial area in Chicago' (by the 1920s).
contradictory_evidence: None on the substance; the ORIGINAL METRIC and PRIMARY SOURCE remain untraced (sibling graded this PROVISIONAL on weaker corroboration).
evidence: Three independent corroborators: (1) Neighborhood Banks designation report: 'quickly became the second busiest commercial area in Chicago' during 1920s; (2) Canaan Baptist Church designation report: 'becoming the second busiest commercial area in Chicago by the 1920s'; (3) LISC 2005: 'Centered around 63rd and Halsted was the second busiest shopping district in Chicago'.
notes: Grade lifted from sibling's PROVISIONAL to SUPPORTED by this brief's new government-document corroboration. Root metric still unknown.
source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Reports (Neighborhood Banks; Canaan Baptist Church of Christ Building) + LISC Englewood Quality of Life Plan (2005)

claim: Elevated and interurban transit expansion drove the development of the 63rd & Halsted commercial district in the early 1900s.
evidence: chicago-l.org: 'The area began attracting retail businesses in the early 1900s with the expansion of the elevated and interurban transit lines' (via Neighborhood Banks designation report echo; chicago-l.org names Evergreen Plaza, automobiles, and other factors for later prominence loss).
notes: Causal-direction claim: transit made commerce, the brief's central causal argument.

claim: In 1964 the Chicago Department of Urban Renewal designated the 63rd & Halsted shopping district an urban renewal area; Mayor Richard J. Daley dedicated the Englewood Shopping Center (pedestrian mall) in 1969.
contradictory_evidence: Sibling had pedestrian-mall chronology as UNRESOLVED (1969 vs ~1973); chicago-l.org supports 1969 dedication. LISC 2005 corroborates 1964 designation.
evidence: chicago-l.org station history: designation 1964; plans for pedestrian mall; Daley dedication 1969; bypass ring road, buses on old streets, sidewalk canopies; spearheaded by Englewood Business Men's Association.
notes: Resolves sibling's 1969-vs-~1973 ambiguity in favor of 1969 (dedication), though mall reopening/end date remains UNRESOLVED.

claim: The Englewood pedestrian mall 'did not work — and perhaps exacerbated the problem.'
contradictory_evidence: None; 'exacerbated' is the author's judgment, not an established causal finding.
evidence: chicago-l.org: 'In the end, the project did not work -- and perhaps exacerbated the problem -- and the district continued to decline.' LISC: 'It didn't work.'
notes: Useful for the competing-interpretations section; do not present 'exacerbated' as proven.

claim: WVON launched April 1, 1963, when Leonard and Phil Chess (Chess Records) bought WHFC-1450 AM; original on-air roster included Franklin McCarthy, E. Rodney Jones, Herb Kent, Wesley South, and Pervis Spann.
evidence: Congressional Record tribute; corroborated by IL House resolution. Corroborates sibling's launch date.
notes: Government record; high-quality corroboration of sibling finding.
source: Congressional Record, Vol. 159, House, pp. H2072-H2073 ('WVON Radio's 50th Anniversary,' Rep. Danny K. Davis, April 2013); Illinois House Resolution HR0201 (98th GA)

claim: WVON was 'the voice during the civil rights movement'; its personalities 'called for calm and peace' during the unrest after Dr. King's assassination and were listened to.
contradictory_evidence: None; celebratory congressional language should be read as attributed, but the station's civil-rights role is multi-sourced.
evidence: Rep. Davis tribute text.
notes: Supports the media-node function claim.

claim: McKie Fitzhugh — owner of McKie's Disc Jockey Show Lounge (6323 S. Cottage Grove, 1955-66) — was on WVON's on-air roster.
evidence: Congressional Record lists 'McKee Fitzhugh' among the Good Guys roster; sibling documents McKie Fitzhugh as Black owner of McKie's club.
notes: New finding of this brief: a documented club-to-radio link inside the corridor's Black cultural economy.
source: Congressional Record, Vol. 159, pp. H2072-H2073 (roster list); CTL-DR-PLACE-001 (club ownership)

claim: Streetcars ran on 63rd (Cottage Grove-Dorchester 1888; Halsted-Ashland 1889; electrified 1893-1899; extended west to Central Park Ave by 1902) and were abandoned May 24, 1953.
evidence: Sibling: early detail PROVISIONAL (single source, chicagorailfan.com); abandonment VERIFIED.
notes: Grades split: abandonment VERIFIED; pre-1900 details PROVISIONAL.

claim: El station openings along/over 63rd: 61st St. Jan 22, 1893; Madison Ave (later Dorchester) and Lexington Ave (later University) Apr 23, 1893; fairgrounds terminal May 12, 1893 (closed Oct 31, 1893); Englewood branch staged 1905-1907, Loomis terminal Jul 13, 1907; Ashland/63rd replaced Loomis May 6, 1969.
contradictory_evidence: None; sibling's red team notes station dates are largely Wikipedia-only elsewhere in the package, but these were verified.
evidence: Sibling graded VERIFIED.
notes: Halsted station opening date remains UNRESOLVED (not included here).

claim: Transit withdrawal: Dorchester station closed Jan 13, 1973; Jackson Park branch truncated Mar 4, 1982 (restored to University Dec 12, 1982); Green Line closed Jan 9, 1994-May 12, 1996, reopened truncated to Cottage Grove; structure east of Cottage Grove demolished Sept 27, 1997 with <24 hours' public notice over community objection led by Rev. Arthur Brazier.
contradictory_evidence: None on dates; the retrospective 'planning mistake' judgment is PROVISIONAL.
evidence: Sibling graded all VERIFIED.
notes: The corridor's most precisely documented functional change.

claim: ~15 jazz clubs on/near 63rd are verified via Chicago Defender citations compiled in UChicago Library's 'Researching Chicago Jazz Venues' guide.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED: Crown Propeller Lounge (868 E. 63rd, 1951-59); Kitty Kat Club (611 E. 63rd); Harry's Show Lounge (432 E. 63rd); Stage Lounge (1524 E. 63rd); Basin Street (6312 S. Cottage Grove); McKie's (6323 S. Cottage Grove, 1955-66); Pershing complex.
notes: Black ownership documented only for McKie's (McKie Fitzhugh) and Basin Street part-owner Eddie 'Cleanhead' Vinson — not inferred elsewhere.

claim: Ahmad Jamal's landmark 1958 'But Not for Me' recordings were made at the Pershing (Budland); Charlie Parker played the Pershing Ballroom in 1950.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Corroborates the entertainment-PRODUCTION function (recordings made on the corridor).

claim: 63rd Street was the southern edge of the Black Belt, 1920-1930 (LaSalle-31st-lake-63rd).
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Boundary-function claim.

claim: Carl Hansberry's purchase at 6140 S. Rhodes broke the Woodlawn Property Owners Association's 1928 covenant in Hansberry v. Lee (1940), giving the NAACP momentum toward Shelley v. Kraemer (1948).
evidence: Sibling: covenant PROVISIONAL; case and Shelley linkage VERIFIED.
notes: Legal-function claim.

claim: The July 29, July 31, and August 5, 1966 open-housing marches centered on 63rd Street — Halverson Realty at 63rd & Kedzie, and Dr. King's rock-struck march toward a 63rd Street real-estate office.
contradictory_evidence: Sibling notes the July 29 Halverson Realty march is a single secondary source (uncertainty carried).
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Civic-arena function: marches happened ON 63rd Street itself.

claim: The Woodlawn Organization, with spokesman/president Rev. Arthur M. Brazier, defeated the University of Chicago's 1963 Woodlawn expansion.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Civic-production function: the corridor's signature political-institutional victory.

claim: Sears at 63rd & Halsted closed January 1976 (Tribune documented split merchant reactions the same week); construction date disputed: 1929 ($1.5M) vs. 1934 (seven stories, fully air-conditioned); exact street address unresolved.
contradictory_evidence: Two conflicting construction accounts; new research did not resolve.
evidence: Sibling: closure VERIFIED; construction DISPUTED; address UNRESOLVED.
notes: Preserved as a dispute per sibling's red team.

claim: The Chicago City Bank and Trust Co. Building, 815 W. 63rd (completed 1930; architect Abraham Epstein; Art Deco; cornerstone 1929) stood 'in the heart of Englewood's bustling commercial district at 63rd and Halsted.'
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED construction facts; landmark designation report (new retrieval) independently corroborates cornerstone 1929 and commercial context. NPS nomination's Chicago Landmark-status assertion still needs ordinance date (PROVISIONAL).
notes: New corroboration of a sibling finding.
source: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 + City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report (Neighborhood Banks)

claim: Daley's Restaurant (1892-present) is the corridor's oldest continuous business.
contradictory_evidence: Current address disputed (6257 S. Cottage Grove vs. 809 E. 63rd).
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED; moved 2019 into Woodlawn Station.
notes: Continuity-function counterweight to the decline narrative.

claim: Population: Englewood 97,595 (1960) -> 24,369 (2020); Woodlawn 81,279 -> 24,425. Englewood ~69% Black in 1960 -> 99% by 1980; West Englewood 48.3% -> 97.5% Black in one decade (1970-80); Chicago Lawn 0% Black in 1970 -> majority by 2000.
contradictory_evidence: Englewood 1920 population: LISC 139,000 vs community-area 86,619 — DISPUTED (not included in this claim).
evidence: Sibling: 'VERIFIED as quoted' via community-area tables; direct Census/API re-verification is a Phase 2 task.
notes: Graded SUPPORTED here (not VERIFIED) because sibling flags figures as quoted-via-secondary pending Census API re-verification.

claim: Chicago Lawn's western 63rd Street segment retains documented commercial vitality and must not be folded into the eastern corridor's decline narrative.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Guardrail claim against selection/geographic bias.

claim: HOLC area D74 (35th-67th, State to Cottage Grove) was graded 'hazardous' with explicitly racist rationale — Washington Park 'almost completely monopolized by the colored race.'
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Policy-function claim (redlining as corridor-shaping force).

claim: No verifiable evidence was found of Black-owned banks, insurers, doctors, dentists, lawyers, or real-estate offices on the corridor, 1940s-1970s.
contradictory_evidence: None — but this is a gap in evidence, not evidence of absence.
evidence: Sibling searched web sources and found nothing verifiable; city directories and Defender ad archives not yet searched.
notes: This brief's largest named evidence gap for the services function; must not be narrated as 'there were none.'

claim: The Green Line's two terminals serving the corridor today are Ashland/63rd and Cottage Grove.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Present-day transit-function anchor.

claim: Hyde Park Township (organized 1861) and Lake Township were both annexed to Chicago in 1889 under the state annexation act approved April 25, 1889.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED (incl. Chicago v. City of Chicago, 143 Ill. 641 (1892)).
notes: Context claim; the street's own platting date is UNRESOLVED (not claimed).

claim: White City Amusement Park (63rd & South Park) operated 1905-1934 (rink to 1958); the Tivoli Theatre (63rd & Cottage Grove) opened Feb 16, 1921, 3,520 seats, closed 1963; the Trianon Ballroom (6201 S. Cottage Grove) opened Dec 6, 1922, demolished 1967.
contradictory_evidence: Tivoli address 6323 vs 6325 S. Cottage Grove DISPUTED (not included).
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Entertainment-district anchors.

claim: The Washington Park National Bank Building (6300 S. Cottage Grove, completed 1924) was acquired by the Cook County Land Bank in 2018; redevelopment approved 2023 with facades preserved and $5M city grant; construction status unresolved as of September 2026.
evidence: Sibling: completion/provisional; acquisition VERIFIED; 2023 approval SUPPORTED; construction status UNRESOLVED.
notes: Contested re-anchoring evidence.

claim: Rev. Arthur M. Brazier pastored Apostolic Church of God (6320 S. Dorchester) 1960-2008 and led both the TWO victory and the 1994 anti-demolition fight.
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Five-decade civic-anchoring function embodied in one person.

claim: Kennedy-King College's 40-acre campus at 63rd & Halsted was dedicated July 18, 2007 (~$192M; 48% credit-enrollment jump).
evidence: Sibling VERIFIED.
notes: Re-anchoring: college campus replacing the failed mall site.
